1.pericope_label: Job resumed his parable and swore by the living God, who had taken away his judgment, that while his breath remained his lips would speak no falsehood; far be it from him to justify his friends, and until death he would not remove his integrity nor let his righteousness go, his heart reproaching him for none of his days

schools.summary: Gill has Job pausing for Zophar, whose turn it was to rise, and the three keeping silence either from a judgment that he was past conviction or a suspicion that he was right; he counts the formula a true oath after Jarchi, sworn by the living God as against breathless idols and deified heroes who were only dead men, presses the point that the falsehood forbidden runs inward, since Job will not speak wickedly of himself by confessing a hypocrisy he cannot find, and distinguishes the thing held fast from any plea at the bar of heaven, which belongs to the living Redeemer, so that what is gripped is the justice of his cause and not a verdict on his friends' state before God.

Henry hears in the title of the discourse the word used for Solomon's proverbs and a root meaning to rule, and catches a note of triumph over opponents now baffled; he calls the clause about judgment taken away speaking hardly and unbecomingly, recalling Elihu's rebuke that God takes away no man's right; he builds the matter of the oath on the frailty of the breath, so that resolutions against sin should be resolutions for life, though in doubtful things it is never safe to be peremptory; and he makes perseverance in uprightness the best preparative for dying, warning that to silence the heart's reproach when it has cause is to affront God, whose deputy conscience is, while to silence it with integrity standing baffles the whisper that asks if thou be the Son of God.

Clarke follows Parkhurst to the same root and finds a matching boldness, a man treating his friends with little ceremony; he judges the complaint a great want of reverence, an irritation bordering on bitterness that cannot be excused, since no man should speak so of his Maker; he hears Adam behind the breath in the nostrils, the principle by which dust became a living and rational creature, so that the clause means while I live and reason; and he rests the closing protest on John's word that if our heart condemn us not we have confidence toward God. Wesley gives the discourse in four words as grave and weighty, and splits the difference on the complaint, that God knows his integrity yet will not plead his cause against his friends.

Ellicott alone reads the complaint as faith rather than murmur, the sufferings being laid on Job for purposes veiled from him, and he maps the speech so named as running on to the chapter on wisdom and the protest of chapter 31. Keil and Delitzsch mark the idiom of the resumption, the lifting up of a mashal on the analogy of Balaam's oracles, deny that the fourth verse is a vow at all and call it instead the agreement of a confession already made with the abiding fact, render its close with Renan, and name the thing held fast tummah, wholeness of character.

Gregory the Great takes the term for a likeness rather than a victory, refuses to hear in it any musical instrument since music in mourning is as a tale out of season, and holds that Scripture folds mystical matter into plain narration so that the obscurity may prick the reader toward a deeper sense.

debates.question: What does the word rendered parable mean here?

sides.position: a grave and weighty discourse spoken with authority, from a root meaning to rule, carrying a note of triumph over opponents now baffled
a likeness, and certainly not a musical instrument, since music in mourning is as a tale out of season
elevated and figurative speech, the lifting up of a mashal on the analogy of Balaam’s oracles

debates.question: Was the charge that God had taken away his judgment defensible?

sides.position: no: it is speaking hardly and unbecomingly, a want of reverence bordering on bitterness that no man should use of his Maker
yes: it is faith rather than complaint, seeing that unexplained sufferings are laid on him for purposes veiled from him
a grievance only, that God knows his integrity and still will not plead his cause against his friends

debates.question: What is the righteousness Job refuses to let go?

sides.position: not a justifying righteousness before God, which no man clings to who has seen its insufficiency, but the justice of his cause
tummah, wholeness or purity of character, which he will not put away from him until he expires
the conscience and credit of an unbroken life, perseverance in which is the best preparative for dying

outliers: Gregory the Great alone argues from the word to a rule of reading, that obscurities mixed into plain narration are meant to prick the reader toward a deeper sense.
Keil and Delitzsch alone deny that the fourth verse is a vow, reading it as a confession already made and now simply agreeing with the fact.
themes: a silence the friends would not break
an oath sworn by the living God
a complaint the expositors cannot excuse
integrity held fast to the last

7.pericope_label: Let mine enemy be as the wicked: for what is the hope of the hypocrite when God taketh away his soul? Will God hear his cry when trouble comes, will he delight himself in the Almighty, will he always call upon God?

schools.summary: Gill reads the imprecation as a disclaimer, since no good man can really wish anyone wicked and the wish would be needless, whoever hates the upright being so already, as the Chaldeans and Sabeans had proved on Job's herds; his chaneph is the religious dissembler who seems what he is not, professes what he has not and worships to be seen, whose expectation is the spider's web and the giving up of the ghost, resting on his substance; he denies that the cry will be heard, the foolish virgins' words returning unanswered while the same God hears his own people in life and in death, and he itemises what such a man cannot love, omnipotence able to destroy soul and body, omniscience that reads the covert heart, and a holiness he does not want.

Henry hears a proverb behind the imprecation, cousin to Daniel's word that the dream be to those who hate thee, and would sooner be a beggar, an outlaw or a galley-slave than stand where the ungodly stand in their pomp; he works the eighth verse as an audit, conceding the gain, since Jehu got a kingdom by dissembling and the Pharisees many a widow's house, and striking down the inference when external profession and privilege are pleaded and overruled with Depart from me, I know you not; he allows one exception to the refused prayer, that true repentance is heard at any hour, and otherwise lines up the texts in which prayer is refused, iniquity regarded in the heart, idols set up, an ear turned from the law; and he presses delight as the test, since nobody perseveres in what gives no pleasure.

Clarke dissents on the imprecation, taking it for a demand that his accuser be proved a lying and perjured man who has charged him with what he cannot prove; he calls the English rendering of chaneph most improper, the Hebrew meaning a defiled wretch and a rascal who sticks at nothing, here a rogue who made his fortune by overreaching and cheating, and he lists the alternatives he will not take, the Chaldee's detractor with the mammon of unrighteousness, the Septuagint's query whether hoping in the Lord will save such a man, and Good's conjecture that God should keep him in quiet; on the taking away he has the righteous man yield up his spirit while this one must have it forced out of the body, and he borrows Blair's picture of the frantic soul racing round the walls of her clay tenement, shrieking for help at every avenue. Wesley says the imprecation in the first person, abhorring the thought of such practice and able to devise no heavier mischief for a foe.

Ellicott keeps the tone cool, the prosperity of the ungodly admitted and not envied; he renders chaneph the godless and reshapes the question as what is his hope, though he get him gain, when God taketh away his soul; and against the man who cannot delight in the Almighty he sets the one who asks whom have I in heaven but thee, noting that this other has no promise to plead and so no assurance of access.

debates.question: What is the force of let mine enemy be as the wicked?

sides.position: a disclaimer: the heaviest thing he could wish anyone, and therefore proof that he has no liking for the condition
not a wish at all but a demand, that his accuser be proved a lying and perjured man
a disavowal of envy, wanting only his adversaries to be like the prosperous ungodly man

debates.question: What does the word translated hypocrite mean?

sides.position: the religious dissembler, who seems what he is not and worships to be seen of men
not a hypocrite at all, but a defiled wretch and a rogue enriched by overreaching and cheating
the godless

debates.question: How should the eighth verse be rendered?

sides.position: with the Authorised Version, when God taketh away his soul, the words our Lord had in eye about gaining the world and losing oneself
what is the hope of the godless, though he get him gain, when God taketh away his soul

outliers: Clarke alone reads the clause as a demand against an accuser rather than a wish about the wicked.
Clarke alone brings in a poet, borrowing Blair's deathbed from The Grave for the soul forced out of its clay tenement.
themes: a curse no good man may utter
a word the translators chose badly
a gain that buys no hope
worship kept up while the hot fit lasts

11.pericope_label: I will teach you by the hand of God, and will not conceal what is with the Almighty; you have all seen it yourselves, so why are you altogether vain? This is the portion of a wicked man with God and the heritage of oppressors: if his children be multiplied, it is for the sword, and his offspring shall not be satisfied with bread

schools.summary: Gill takes the hand of God for providence rather than nature, the chapter before having displayed creation while the harder lesson now promised is why the upright are afflicted and the godless left at ease, and he holds the teacher no less fit for the office in calamity than in wealth, adversity having been his school; he points at the evidence the friends' own eyes had furnished, the ungodly spreading like a green bay tree while better men laboured, with the speaker himself a case in front of them; he pushes the portion past death to the second death and the company of devils and dissemblers; and he observes that many children are common to good and bad, Haman leaving ten sons and Ahab seventy.

Henry draws a rule from the teacher's position, that we must not disdain to learn even from those who are sick and poor, yea, and peevish too, if what they deliver is true and good; he maps the agreement and the quarrel, both sides holding that cruelty will be reckoned with while the three maintained, verse by verse, that the reckoning falls visibly and soon, pain all their days, the destroyer in their prosperity, the branch not green, the end before its time, so that Job's correction is about timing, the stroke often deferred and a reprieve no pardon; and he sees in a numerous, well-settled family only more and fairer marks for the three arrows of sword, famine and pestilence, war's sword for those bred to live by it, or justice's, or the murderer's for the estate, and for the rest a poverty with neither enough nor what they were used to.

Clarke reads the teaching formula as a disclaimer of originality, nothing out of his own head and nothing quoted but speech under divine assistance, notes the Chaldee's bolder by the prophecy of God and prefers Good's concerning the dealings of God; he lingers on the rebuke hebel tehbalu, which Good turns into why should ye thus babble babblings and which he would gladly render vanitize vanity if English allowed; and he keeps a middle course on the portion, the displeasure often shown where men can see it and at other times held over, lest anyone forget that perdition and recompense are both coming. Wesley has it in a line, that they are vain to condemn an afflicted man.

Keil and Delitzsch make the twelfth verse the pivot of the chapter, the emphatic pronoun meaning not merely all of you but your very selves, so that Job concedes what he had seemed to deny, that as a rule the oppressor's end is what the three described, while what remains false is the application to a man who does not carry the marks. Ellicott refers the sight to something else, the power of God just proclaimed, renders the formula of the hand of God or what is in God's power, and raises the question whether the rest of the chapter is Job's at all, since some have supposed it the missing third speech of Zophar with the rubric dropped; he will not have it, what the arrangement gains in symmetry being lost in drama, and he explains the one remarkable thing, that the speaker takes up precisely Zophar's closing words, by Job accepting his friends' facts entire while refusing their inference.

debates.question: What is it that they themselves have all seen?

sides.position: the evil-doer's lot, which Job here concedes to be the rule, the clause being the pivot on which everything after it turns
the power of God, which Job had just finished proclaiming
what their own observation had furnished, the ungodly in affluence and better men in affliction, with Job himself before their eyes

debates.question: When does the portion of a wicked man fall due?

sides.position: after death: not what he has in this life, often affluent, but the second death and a portion with hypocrites
in this life, but often deferred, the stroke falling slowly and surely, a reprieve being no pardon
sometimes shown where men can see it, sometimes reserved for another world

outliers: Ellicott alone raises the conjecture that the rest of the chapter is the missing third speech of Zophar, the rubric having dropped out, and refuses it because what the arrangement gains in symmetry it loses in drama.
Keil and Delitzsch alone make the twelfth verse the pivot on which the reading of everything after it turns.
Clarke alone wishes English would let him render the rebuke vanitize vanity.
themes: a teacher in the middle of his affliction
a concession and a refused inference
a portion reckoned with God rather than with men
children multiplied into targets

15.pericope_label: Those that remain of him shall be buried in death and his widows shall not weep; though he heap up silver as the dust and prepare raiment as the clay, the just shall put it on and the innocent divide the silver; he buildeth his house as a moth and as a booth the keeper maketh; the rich man shall lie down but not be gathered, he openeth his eyes and he is not

schools.summary: Gill reads the heap of silver as a portrait of appetite, a man who cannot be content without amassing; he lets the moth eat itself out of house and home and be brushed away at last, notes a rendering that makes the palace a thing among the stars, and applies the figures to a confidence of spider's web, moth-eaten cloth and sand; on the rich man lying down he offers a sleepless alternative, the abundance and the fear of losing it refusing to let him settle.

Henry watches the heaping until, as James says, the silver is cankered and the garments moth-eaten: death will strip him, and the robe he laid up will be worn by the just while the innocent share out the metal, providence disposing of estates as it pleases and often making men's wills against their wills, the Egyptians' jewels being Israel's pay, while the new owners spread rather than hoard, money being like manure and good for nothing unless it is spread; he adds the tenant's security, a moth with no apprehension of danger whose place shall know him no more; and he develops the last verse into a man lying down in his riches as in a strong city whom the world calls happy, full of tossings to and fro till dawn, his cares feeding his fears, so that we follow him to bed and do not find him at ease.

Clarke reads buried in death as the strongest thing the words can carry, death itself the place where such a man lies with no redemption and no rising, and he rejects the Chaldee's entombed in corruption, which entombs high and low alike; he moralises the instrument rather than the amount, money being the readiest agent for good or ill, so that its abuser is doubly cursed and its right user doubly blessed; he admires the skill of the building and then dissolves it, the insect's lodging belonging to the caterpillar state and lasting only until the change, and the watchman's booth, run up of the lightest materials to shade him while the grapes ripen, left to the winter rains; and on the last verse he lays out two readings he will not pretend are one, the grave with neither a respectable interment among men nor a gathering with the righteous, behind which lies the old notion that the unburied wander and find no rest, and a waking in this world to find a hostile tribe has carried off the whole. Wesley has the moth crushed in the garment and the shed pulled down as suddenly as it rose, explains the plural widows by polygamy and their dry eyes by the tyranny endured, and ends with a carcase like dung instead of an honourable grave with his fathers.

Keil and Delitzsch hear the pestilence in the verb of burial, third of the strokes that fall one after another, find the clause shared with Asaph's psalm, and hold that the blows come too fast for the customary rites. Ellicott keeps it quieter, the end obscure and itself a burial into oblivion; he offers hired mourning-women or the wives of the survivors for the widows, and lets the gathering of the last verse be of the wealth rather than the man, so that he opens his eyes and it is gone.

debates.question: What does buried in death mean?

sides.position: literally: death itself is the place where he lies, with no redemption and no rising, and the Chaldee’s entombed in corruption is refused as entombing high and low alike
buried by the pestilence, the third of the strokes that sweep away the evil-doer and his family
an obscure end exciting no sympathy, a death that is itself a burial into oblivion

debates.question: Who are his widows, and why do they not weep?

sides.position: his own, for such men had many wives, and dry-eyed because they had groaned under his tyranny and are glad to be delivered
either the women hired to make lamentation, or the wives of the survivors
the women he leaves behind, kept from the usual rites because the blows fall stroke after stroke and the shock stifles pity

debates.question: What is it that shall not be gathered?

sides.position: the man: neither a respectable interment among men nor a gathering with the righteous
his store, which he adds nothing more to, lying down sure of it and waking stripped
his wealth: he opens his eyes and it is gone
his mind, never composed and settled enough to enjoy what he has, so that his abundance will not suffer him to sleep

outliers: Clarke alone sets two readings of the last verse side by side and refuses to pretend they are one, preferring the grave while keeping the waking to a plundered house as a real alternative, and noting it to be precisely what had happened to the speaker.
Gill alone reports a rendering that makes the palace a thing among the stars.
Henry alone makes money's worth depend on its being spread, like manure.
themes: survivors nobody mourns
silver heaped for other men to wear
a house as brittle as a moth's
a bed that gives no rest

20.pericope_label: Terrors take hold on him as waters, a tempest stealeth him away in the night; the east wind carrieth him away and he departeth, and as a storm hurleth him out of his place; for God shall cast upon him and not spare, though he would fain flee out of his hand; men shall clap their hands at him and hiss him out of his place

schools.summary: Gill hears in the flood image both the deathbed and what follows, a guilty memory running back over old sins, the law's curses alighting, the fury of the Almighty surrounding him and devils for company, terror on every side, a Magor-missabib rolling on without ceasing; he prefers the burning wind of the Septuagint and Vulgate and quotes Thevenot for the blast that gives a man time only to say he burns before he drops; he fills out the casting with sins laid on the conscience as an intolerable weight, wrath poured like fire and punishment pressing like a talent of lead, from one who spared neither the sinning angels nor the old world nor Sodom; and he will not let the clapping be cruelty, since the righteous indulge no evil passion but rejoice in the glory of justice, a company he would widen to the angels or else read the verb impersonally.

Henry splits the reaction to the terrors in two, a silent and sullen despair in which the storm steals the man away at night with nobody aware of it, or an open and clamorous one in which he is hurled from his place with noise, death being a fair gale to carry the godly home and an east wind to hurry the other off; on the casting he holds there is no flying from it and no bearing up under it, the gates locked, the gulf fixed and rocks and mountains vainly called on for shelter, so that those who will not flee now to the arms of grace will not be able to flee from the arms of wrath; and he has the judgments applauded and the name left with perpetual marks of infamy, laughed at where he had been caressed and cried up, his ashes trampled.

Clarke keeps to the tempest in the night, where darkness half hides the danger and the way out; he names the east wind with a sailor's word as a levanter, the euroclydon that wrecked Paul, and would delete the supplied subject of the casting outright, keeping the storm of the verses before as the agent, so that it shall fall on him and not spare, and flying from its power he shall continue to fly; he personifies the weather to the last, letting the storm clap and shriek the man off the stage, and explains the gesture from an old practice of hissing an officer out of a post he has disgraced. Wesley gives the simile a river breaking its banks with the wrath coming unexpectedly like a thief, repeats Henry's sentence about the arms of grace and of wrath almost word for word, takes the casting for darts or plagues one after another, and reads the clapping of onlookers as joy at the removal of a public pest, astonishment and plain contempt.

Keil and Delitzsch are most informative on the wind: the qadim out of the Arabian desert is the destructive and parching wind of the language and goes now by another name, the wind from the sunrise, rare in summer and frequent in winter, burning up the young growth if it holds so that a year of famine follows, which is why Lebanon calls it by a word that has come to mean poisonous but first meant devastating; and they add what it does to a body, blood excited, chest contracted, restlessness and bad dreams, man and beast feeling sickly while it lasts. Ellicott dissents on the subject of the casting, which may be the man who spent his life fleeing from the tyrant's power and is now only too glad to avenge himself.

debates.question: Who casts upon him and does not spare?

sides.position: God, as the Authorised Version supplies: sins laid on the conscience, wrath poured like fire, a day of patience now over
the man who had spent his life fleeing from his power, now only too glad of the chance to avenge himself
the storm of the preceding verses, the supplied subject being struck out altogether

debates.question: What is the east wind that carries him away?

sides.position: the qadim out of the Arabian desert, now called the wind from the sunrise, dry and parching, sickening to man and beast while it lasts
the burning wind of the Septuagint and the Vulgate, which gives a man time only to say he burns before he drops
a levanter, the euroclydon of the shipwreck in Acts
some terrible judgment, the east wind being the most vehement and pernicious of those parts

debates.question: Who claps the hands and hisses him from his place?

sides.position: the storm, personified, driving him off the stage as a disgraced officer is hissed from his post
onlookers, in joy at the removal of a public pest, in astonishment and in contempt, leaving perpetual marks of infamy on his name
the righteous and the angels, rejoicing not in the scene but in the glory of justice, or else the verb read impersonally

outliers: Clarke alone would strike the supplied subject from both closing verses and let the storm itself cast, clap and hiss.
Keil and Delitzsch alone describe what the wind does to a body, and what it is called now in Syria and in Lebanon.
Gill alone refuses to let the clapping be read as cruelty, and would widen the company to the angels or take the verb impersonally.
themes: terrors coming in like water
a wind out of the desert
no shelter from what is cast down
hands clapped and a man hissed from his place
